prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

That dusty bubble gum, once ubiquitous as starlings, is no more, my love. Whistling dinosaurs now populate only animation studios, the furious actions of angels causing their breasts to flop out in mannerist frescos flake away as sleet holds us in its teeth. And the bus-station's old urinals go under the grindstone and the youthful spelunkers graduate into the wrinkle-causing sun. The sea seemingly a constant to the naked eye is one long goodbye, perpetually the tide recedes, beaches dotted with debris. Unto each is given a finite number of addresses, ditties to dart the heart to its moments of sorrow and swoon. The sword's hilt glints, the daffodils bow down, all is temporary as a perfect haircut, a kitten in the lap, yet sitting here with you, my darling, waiting for a tuna melt and side of slaw seems all eternity I'll ever need and all eternity needs of me.

outputs.L2: That powdery stick of gum, formerly as common as flocks of starlings, has vanished, my darling. Dinosaurs that once whistled survive only within the walls of cartoon houses; the frantic movements of angels—the ones whose bosoms spilled free across those overwrought Renaissance ceilings—crumble away while frozen rain grips us tightly. Meanwhile, the antiquated urinals in the bus depot are ground down to nothing, and the young cave-explorers age their way out into the daylight that etches lines on skin. The ocean, which to a casual glance appears unchanging, is truly one endless farewell, its waters forever pulling back, its shores littered with wreckage. Each person receives only so many homes, only so many small tunes to prick the heart toward its instants of grief and giddiness. The handle of the blade catches the light, the daffodils dip their heads, everything as fleeting as a flawless trim, a small cat resting on your knees—and yet here I am beside you, my love, awaiting a tuna melt with a helping of coleslaw, and this feels like every scrap of forever I could want, and every scrap of forever that could ever want me.

# On Impermanence and the Sufficiency of Love

Everything that once felt familiar and seemingly permanent eventually fades and disappears. Consider the small pleasures and fixtures of ordinary life—the sweet taste of bubble gum from childhood, the towering dinosaurs that once ruled the earth, even the worn old urinals in a forgotten public building. Each seemed, in its moment, like a constant feature of the world. Yet none of them endured. Time, indifferent and relentless, carries all such things away, leaving behind only traces and memories.

The sea offers a fitting emblem of this truth. To the casual observer, it appears eternal and unchanging, a vast and steady presence stretching to the horizon. But the sea is, in reality, a symbol of perpetual change and loss. Its tides advance and endlessly recede, forever reshaping the shoreline, forever depositing debris upon the sand. What looks like permanence is, on closer inspection, ceaseless motion and quiet erosion.

We ourselves are bound by these same laws. Each of us is granted only a finite existence, a brief span punctuated by fleeting moments of sorrow and joy. Our lives are measured and limited, our sufferings and delights alike passing quickly, giving way one to another until our allotted time is spent.

From this we may draw a difficult but honest conclusion: all things in life, no matter how beautiful, are inherently temporary. Nothing precious is exempt from this rule. Beauty does not purchase permanence; if anything, it makes the loss more keenly felt.

And yet, in the face of such universal transience, there remains a quiet consolation. For despite knowing that everything must pass, a single, simple, loving moment shared with someone dear feels like eternity enough. In the presence of a beloved, the fleeting becomes sufficient, and the awareness of impermanence no longer diminishes the moment but deepens its worth. That, for the speaker, is all the forever one could ever need.
outputs.L4:
# The Nature of Impermanence

Everything passes. This is the quiet, insistent truth that runs beneath the surface of our days like water wearing away stone. Consider the ordinary miracle of bubble gum—that bright pink globe swelling with breath, holding its shape for one triumphant instant before it bursts and collapses into nothing. It is a small thing, almost comic, and yet it rehearses the same drama that has played out across geological time.

The dinosaurs, too, once ruled this earth with their enormous bodies and their appetites, thundering across continents that no longer exist in the shapes they knew. Now they are bones in museum halls, oil in the ground, the faintest echo pressed into ancient rock. If creatures so vast could vanish, what hope of permanence remains for anything?

Even the oceans, which we imagine as endless and eternal, are only borrowed water. They rise and evaporate, they crash against shorelines they will one day abandon, retreating and advancing across millennia we cannot feel. The flowers understand this best of all—they bloom in brilliant defiance of their own brevity, unfolding their colors precisely because they cannot last. By evening the petals brown at the edges; by week's end they have surrendered to the soil.

And we are no exception. Our own lives, which feel so central and unshakable to us, are subject to the same relentless arithmetic of loss. We age. We forget. We are forgotten in turn. The passage of time spares nothing—not the smallest sweetness nor the mightiest beast, not the sea itself nor the tender human heart that longs so desperately to hold on.

Faced with this catalog of decay, one might expect despair. If nothing endures, then what is the point of loving anything, of building anything, of hoping for permanence in a universe designed for erasure?

But here the poem turns, and its wisdom arrives not with grand philosophy but with the humblest of scenes. The speaker sits across a diner table from someone beloved. There is a plate of food, unremarkable and ordinary. There is the low hum of conversation, the clink of a fork, the warmth of simply being together in this particular booth on this particular afternoon. And in that moment—this small, unglamorous, entirely temporary moment—the speaker discovers that the hunger for eternity has been satisfied.

This is the poem's central revelation: we have been searching for permanence in all the wrong places. We seek it in objects meant to last, in monuments and possessions and legacies that will inevitably crumble. But meaning was never housed in the enduring thing. It lives instead in the fleeting, in the shared, in the ordinary intimacy of one present moment fully inhabited. To sit with someone you love, to be genuinely *here*, is to touch something that needs no future to justify it. The moment is complete in itself.

And so the transience that first seemed like a curse reveals itself as a gift. Precisely because nothing lasts, everything matters. The bubble bursts, the flower fades, the diner meal ends—and yet within its brief span it offers all the eternity a human heart could ask for.

# The Art of That Whistling Sound

There's something magical about whistling, and it connects people across cultures and generations. That simple act of pursing your lips and pushing air through creates melodies that can express joy, ease loneliness, or simply pass the time.

## Learning That Skill

Many people remember the moment they first mastered whistling. It doesn't come naturally to everyone, and that can be frustrating at first. Children often spend hours trying to produce that perfect note, only to hear nothing but the sound of rushing air. But once you get it, that ability stays with you forever.

## Whistling Through History

Whistling has served many purposes throughout human history. Workers used it to coordinate tasks, and shepherds whistled to communicate with their dogs across great distances. That familiar tune could signal danger, call someone home, or express affection. In some cultures, entire whistled languages developed, allowing people to "speak" across valleys and mountains.

## The Everyday Magic

Consider that moment when you catch yourself whistling without thinking. Maybe you're happy, and the sound just bubbles up naturally. Perhaps you're nervous, and that gentle melody helps calm your nerves. Whistling connects our inner emotions with the world around us, and it does so effortlessly.

## More Than Just Sound

That whistle you hear from a passing stranger might brighten your entire day. And when someone whistles a familiar song, it can transport you to another time and place. This simple human ability reminds us that beauty exists in the smallest gestures, and that we all share this wonderful capacity for musical expression.

So next time you hear that cheerful whistling, take a moment to appreciate it. And maybe, just maybe, join in yourself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about the impermanence of everything, addressed to a lover, ending with a quiet moment together at a diner. Use surreal and unexpected imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Diner Knows

The mountains are only borrowing their shapes
from the sky, my love, the way your hands
borrow their warmth from some furnace
buried in the year we haven't lived yet.

Everything is leaving. Even now
the wallpaper unlearns its roses,
petal by petal releasing them
into the slow amnesia of the walls.

I have watched clocks grow soft as fruit,
watched the ocean pack its blue into a suitcase
and leave without a forwarding address.
Nothing stays. The moths know this—

they eat the coats of our old selves
and grow into the shape of departure.
Your face is a country
that redraws its borders every time you laugh.

Still—

the diner holds us like a held breath.
The neon hums its pink electric hymn.
Your coffee ghosts a small cloud toward the ceiling
where it will forget it was ever coffee.

Outside, the constellations shuffle
and deal themselves new names.
But here, the vinyl booth remembers our weight.
The waitress refills nothing and it is enough.

Let the universe misplace its keys.
Let the moon dissolve like sugar in the dark.
I will hold your hand across the formica
and we will disappear together, slowly,

the way steam does—
first a shape, then a suggestion,
then the warm and nameless
thing that stays.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem meditating on transience—extinction, aging, erosion, the passage of time—that lands on the idea that being with a loved one in an ordinary moment feels like enough eternity.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Hours Keep

The last of a species dies without ceremony, a small folding-inward of the world, one voice subtracted from a chorus no one was counting. Somewhere a river spends a thousand years teaching a canyon how to be empty. Mountains, given time enough, learn to lie down. Everything is leaving—not all at once, which we could grieve, but slowly, which we mostly fail to notice: the coastline retreating a grain at a time, the photograph surrendering its faces to a yellow fog, the language losing its word for a color no one sees anymore.

I have felt time move through my own hands. The knuckles thickening. The way a face in the mirror becomes, year by year, a translation of itself, faithful but no longer exact. We are all being weathered. We are all, quietly, becoming the thing that comes after us.

And still.

This afternoon, the ordinary light comes slantwise through the kitchen. You are peeling an orange, and the smell of it is bright and briefly permanent. You say something I will not remember by evening. I hand you half. Outside, the erosion continues; the extinctions proceed; the stars are dying at their leisurely, catastrophic pace.

But here is the whole of it: your thumb, the torn rind, the wet gold of the fruit, the small warmth of a body that also will not last, held now against the enormous going-away of things.

If eternity is a length of time, we will never have enough of it. But if eternity is a fullness—a moment so complete it forgets to end—then this is it. This is all of it. The clock keeps its opinion. I keep the orange, the light, and you.

It is enough. It is more than enough. It is everything the vanishing world was making room for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write me a love poem that mixes cosmic and mundane imagery, contrasting the vastness of time and loss with a small everyday scene like waiting for lunch at a café.
counterfactuals.output:
# Table for Two at the End of Everything

Galaxies have been dying since before
you asked if I wanted the soup or the salad.
Whole suns collapsed in the time it took
the waiter to forget us by the window,

and still I am undone by the way
you fold the paper napkin into halves,
then quarters, worrying its edge
the way tides worry at a shrinking coast.

Somewhere, light that left its star
when the first fish considered land
is only now arriving—
and you are only now deciding

between the coffee and the tea,
your spoon a small and patient moon
orbiting the saucer's chipped horizon,
and I would wait ten thousand years for this,

for the ordinary miracle of you
reaching across the table for the salt,
your hand a comet I have named
and named again, and cannot bear to lose.

The universe is mostly empty space.
So is the chair across from me
when you step out to take a call—
and in that cold, unbearable arithmetic

I understand at last what physics means:
that everything is falling
toward the thing it loves,
that even light gives up its speed for warmth,

that I have crossed the dark
on the strength of an appetite
no soup could satisfy—
just you, just this, just lunch, just now,

the check arriving like a distant star,
the tip I leave a small apology
to time itself, for how I spent it,
gladly, watching you decide.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, image-dense prose poem about how nothing lasts—dinosaurs, old urinals, tides, haircuts—but concluding that sitting with your darling waiting for a tuna melt is all the eternity you need.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Half-Life of Everything

The dinosaurs are gone, and nobody asked them if they were ready. One long Tuesday the sky filled with fire and the thunder-lizards laid down in the ferns like children told it was bedtime too early, and now they are oil, they are the ghost inside your grandmother's Buick, they are the reason the highway hums.

Nothing lasts. Say it with me. The old urinals of the world are being pried from tiled walls, those porcelain cathedrals where men stood in the sacred silence of not looking at each other, and they are hauled to dumpsters, replaced by sleeker things, by sensors that flush without being asked, and no one holds a funeral for a fixture, though a fixture is a kind of faith—the belief that you will return tomorrow and it will still be there.

The tide takes back what the tide delivers. Every sandcastle is a lease, not a deed. The ocean is a landlord with no mercy and excellent timing, arriving always at the moment the towers are tallest, licking the moats to mud, and the children scream with the specific joy of watching their own work undone, because somewhere we know, even at six years old, that permanence is the joke and impermanence is the punchline.

And your hair—look at it—cut last month into something you loved in the mirror, and already growing out, already becoming a different animal, and one day gone entirely, the way everything leaves by the top of the head first, the way we all quietly go bald under the fluorescent honesty of time.

So nothing lasts.

*But.*

Here is the diner. Here is the vinyl booth, cracked and taped and warm from the afternoon light coming through the smudged glass. Here is the ketchup bottle with its geological rings of dried red. Here is the waitress, patient as weather, who has already turned toward the kitchen. And here, across from me, is you—my darling, my brief and glorious accident—stirring your coffee for no reason, because the sugar dissolved three minutes ago, stirring it just to have something to do with your hands while we wait.

We are waiting for a tuna melt.

That is all. The dinosaurs are dead and the urinals are hauled away and the tide is undoing some child's afternoon and my hair is quietly abandoning me, and none of it, *none of it,* can touch this booth, this light, this smell of griddle and rye, this small forever of you looking up and catching me looking at you.

Let it all pass. Let it all go to oil and sand and salt.

I have everything.

The melt is coming.

I could wait here the rest of my life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem in the style of contemporary American poets that piles up strange, tender images about mortality and impermanence, ending on a tender note to "my love."
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory of the Vanishing**

Someone is always leaving the party early,
coat half on, one arm searching the dark sleeve
of the afternoon. The moths have eaten
a small window in my mother's wedding dress
and through it I can see the next century
already forgetting our names.

I have started to love things
the way you love a glass of water
you didn't know you were thirsty for—
the mailbox, the rusted hinge,
the neighbor's dog barking at nothing,
which is to say, at everything,
which is to say, at time.

Look: the apple browns where the knife touched it.
The snow keeps its appointment and then breaks it.
My grandfather's watch still runs
though the wrist it belonged to
is now a field in Ohio, is now
the idea of a field, is now
the word *field* softening in my mouth
like bread.

Everything is on loan.
The light through the curtain. The ache in the knee.
The particular way you say my name
when you're not fully awake—
half question, half prayer,
a syllable I'll spend
whatever's left of me
memorizing.

So let the vase crack.
Let the peaches go soft in the bowl.
Let the whole impermanent orchestra
tune its instruments toward silence.

I only wanted to tell you
before the leaving, before the last
small window in the dress:
the world is a house on fire
and I would still choose
to stand here in the doorway,
holding the doorknob's brief warmth,

turning back to say
*it's you, it was always you,*
my love, my flammable, my brief.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
